A communist is a person who believes in, supports, or actively works toward a system called communism — a political and economic idea where wealth, land, factories, and all major resources are owned collectively by the community or society as a whole, rather than by private individuals or corporations.

In other words, a communist believes that no single person should "own" the farm, the factory, or the mine. Instead, everyone who works there should collectively own it and share the benefits equally.

To really understand what a communist is, you need to understand the core problem they believe exists in the world.

Communists look at society and see it divided into two broad groups:

  • The owners (capitalists) — people who own factories, land, banks, and businesses. They make money not necessarily by working themselves, but by owning things that others work in.
  • The workers (the proletariat) — people who don't own much, and so must sell their labor to the owners in exchange for a wage.

A communist believes this arrangement is fundamentally unfair. The workers do all the real work — they mine the coal, stitch the clothes, build the cars — but the profits flow mostly to the owners. The worker gets a wage; the owner gets rich. Communists see this as a form of exploitation built into the very structure of society.

Their solution? Abolish private ownership of these major resources entirely. Let society — meaning everyone collectively — own the means of production (factories, farms, mines, etc.), so that the fruits of labor are shared among all.

A communist's end goal is a classless society — a world where there is no "rich class" and no "poor class," because no one privately owns the tools of production. Everyone contributes what they can and receives what they need.

The classic slogan that captures this vision comes from Karl Marx:

"From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs."

This means: you contribute to society based on your talents and capacity, and you receive from society based on what you genuinely need — not based on how much money or property you happen to own.

In this ideal communist society, there would eventually be no state (no government controlling people), no money, no social classes, and no exploitation. Everything would be organized cooperatively.

The modern use of the word "communist" is almost entirely rooted in the work of two 19th-century thinkers: Karl Marx (a German philosopher and economist) and Friedrich Engels (his collaborator). Together they wrote The Communist Manifesto in 1848, which laid out the core arguments for why capitalism was unjust and why workers of the world needed to rise up and take collective control.

Marx also wrote a massive, deeply analytical work called Das Kapital, in which he dissected how capitalism actually functions and argued that it contains the seeds of its own destruction — that eventually, the exploited workers would overthrow the owners and build a new kind of society.

A person who follows these ideas of Marx is also called a Marxist, and Marxism is the intellectual foundation of most communist thought.
Communism vs. Socialism — A Key Distinction

Many learners get confused between communists and socialists, so it's worth clarifying.

Both believe that wealth and resources should be more equally distributed, and both are critical of unregulated capitalism. But:

  • A socialist generally believes that key industries (like healthcare, education, energy) should be publicly owned or heavily regulated, while still allowing private property and markets to exist in other areas. Most socialists work within democratic systems and want gradual reforms.
  • A communist goes further. They want the complete elimination of private ownership of major productive resources and the complete restructuring of society — often believing that the current system cannot simply be reformed but must be fundamentally replaced.

Think of it this way: socialism adjusts the existing system; communism wants to replace it entirely.

The 20th century saw several governments that called themselves communist and were led by communist parties:

  • The Soviet Union (USSR): The world's first communist state, born from the Russian Revolution of 1917, led initially by Vladimir Lenin and later by Joseph Stalin. It lasted until 1991.
  • China: After a revolution in 1949, Mao Zedong led the Communist Party to power. China still calls itself a communist state today, though its economy now has many capitalist elements.
  • Cuba: Fidel Castro established a communist government in 1959, which continues to this day.
  • North Korea: Officially calls itself a socialist state, though it functions with strong communist-derived authoritarian control.

It's important to note that these real-world communist states were often brutal, authoritarian, and in many ways diverged sharply from the idealistic vision Marx had written about. Many people who study communism academically distinguish sharply between "theoretical communism" (the idea as written) and "actually existing communism" (how it played out in practice under leaders like Stalin or Mao, who used mass violence and repression).

Not all communists are the same. Over time, many branches and interpretations developed:

  • Marxist-Leninists follow Marx's ideas as interpreted and applied by Lenin, who believed a disciplined revolutionary party must lead the working class to revolution. This became the dominant form of communism in the Soviet Union.
  • Maoists follow the ideas of Mao Zedong, who adapted communism to an agrarian (farming-based) society like China and emphasized the revolutionary role of the peasantry.
  • Trotskyists follow Leon Trotsky, who opposed Stalin and believed in "permanent revolution" — the idea that communism needed to spread globally to survive, rather than being built in one country first.
  • Libertarian communists or anarcho-communists want a classless, stateless society without any central government at all — they distrust state power even in revolutionary hands.

What unites all of them is the core belief in collective ownership and the eventual elimination of class-based exploitation.
How the Word Is Used Today

The word "communist" is used in several ways in modern life:

  1. As a self-description: Some people genuinely and proudly identify as communists — they read Marxist theory, are members of communist parties (which still exist in many countries), and advocate for revolutionary change.
  2. As a descriptive label: Historians, journalists, and analysts use "communist" to describe governments, parties, or movements that follow or followed communist ideology.
  3. As an insult or slur: Especially in the United States and other Western countries shaped by the Cold War (the decades-long political and ideological conflict between the capitalist West, led by the US, and the communist East, led by the Soviet Union, roughly from 1947 to 1991), "communist" is sometimes used loosely and pejoratively — hurled at anyone whose policies are considered too left-wing, even if those policies have nothing to do with actual communism. In this usage, it's more of an emotional attack than an accurate description.

It's important to separate the word's precise meaning from its emotionally charged, sometimes weaponized use in political debate.

A communist is someone who believes that the root cause of poverty, inequality, and exploitation lies in the private ownership of the economy's productive machinery — and that the solution is to put that ownership into the hands of all people collectively, creating a society built on equality of condition rather than equality of opportunity alone.
